segments.structure: /tat/ [subject, correlative] · /pārameśvaram/ [predicate] · /śrīmat-mahā-ānanda-vijṛmbhitam/ [second predicate] → main clause; copula (asti) understood
segments.concepts: *vijṛmbhita* (vijṛmbhaṇa) — „yawning open, unfolding“: in the Trika the spontaneous self-expansion of consciousness (śakti); with mahānanda, the bliss of the Supreme Lord unfolding itself.

grammar: Two clauses. The first (685) joins a concessive clause — atra mad-vāk aśaktā api, „though my speech is incapable here“ — to a relative clause, yat niyantraṇam ullaset, whose optative generalises („whatever control may shine forth“). The second (686) is the main clause: the correlative tat takes up yat … niyantraṇam and receives two nominal predicates, pārameśvaram and the compound śrīmat-mahā-ānanda-vijṛmbhitam; the copula is understood. The verse is the commentator's humility formula: any mastery in what follows is the Lord's, not his.
translation: Although my speech (vāc) is incapable (aśakta) here, whatever control (niyantraṇa) may shine forth (ullaset) — that belongs to the Supreme Lord (pārameśvara): it is the unfolding (vijṛmbhita) of glorious great bliss (mahānanda).
comparison: All three read the concessive clause alike. They part over niyantraṇa: Dyczkowski takes it as a restriction on the reader's understanding (and adds that it is not the author's fault), DharmaMitra reverses it into „unfettered expression“; the translation here reads control or ordering of the words, which the Lord, not the commentator, brings about.
